title: Sita calls the fire as witness
hookLine: after the war Sita answers Rama, then calls Agni as her witness; why Hindus still make vows before the fire
carry: the fire is the witness of truth
last: SITA KEPT HER DHARMA, EVEN CAPTIVE.

cards: The war is over. Ravana is dead. Sita is brought out in front of the whole army, and the reunion the story has been moving toward doesn't come.

In Valmiki's sixth book, Rama speaks to her coldly, in public. He says, in paraphrase, that he fought to clear his name and his family's, and that she may go wherever she likes. It's a hard scene to read.
Today isn't about defending it or explaining it away. It's about the woman who has to answer it, and what she says.

teach.h: SHE WIPES HER TEARS AND SPEAKS
teach.b: Sita doesn't stay silent. She wipes her tears and speaks, and Valmiki gives her a full answer. In paraphrase: why do you speak to me like this, the way a common man speaks to a common woman?
What was in my power, my heart, was always yours. What was not in my power, my body seized by force, was not my doing. If you meant to give me up, why didn't you say so when Hanuman came?
I would have ended my life then, and spared you a war. Then she asks Lakshmana to build a fire.
She faces the flames and calls on Agni, the god of fire, in paraphrase: as my heart has never strayed from Rama, may Agni, the witness of the world, protect me. And she steps in.
Agni rises carrying her, gives her back, and declares her faultless. Here's the teaching inside the scene.
Agni is the fire of every Vedic offering, and in the epics he is the witness: earlier in this same story, Rama and Sugriva seal their friendship by walking around a fire.
That's why, at a Hindu wedding, the couple circles the sacred fire and make their vows before it; families call it agni sakshi, the fire as witness. Sita didn't ask the army to vouch for her.

She called the witness her whole tradition trusts. The tradition still wrestles with this scene: many read the fire as her victory, and Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas tells it so the real Sita was never in Lanka at all.

how: Sita's ordeal by fire, the agni pariksha, is retold, staged and debated across Hindu traditions; and at Hindu weddings couples still circle the sacred fire, making their vows with Agni as witness.

o: the woman who answers Rama, then calls the fire as her witness
a queen who stays silent and lets Rama speak
a captive who is never asked to answer for anything

games.q: after the war — tap the pairs.
p: names what was in her power
builds the fire at her request
vows made around the sacred fire

s: in Valmiki, Sita says nothing and walks into the fire
she answers Rama at length, asks her own questions, then asks for the fire.
Sita asks why Rama didn't give her up when Hanuman came
she says she'd have ended her life then, and spared him a war.
Hindu couples still make their wedding vows before a sacred fire
the couple circles the fire with Agni as witness, the same witness Sita called.

games.q: at your cousin's wedding, the couple walks around the sacred fire before their vows. by Sita's story, why the fire?
o: Agni is the witness. vows made before him are made before God.
it lights the ceremony, which often runs late.
it's a test of the bride, like Sita's fire.
games.why: Sita called Agni, the witness of the world, before the whole army. at a Hindu wedding, the couple makes their promises before that same witness. it isn't a test of anyone.

practice: Many Hindu homes light a small lamp, a diya, when they pray. Light one, or a candle, somewhere safe, or just picture a flame.

Let it be your witness for a few breaths, and say one true thing before it, silently: something that's yours, that you'd stand behind in front of anyone. If you pray, offer it to God, as Sita offered her truth to Agni.

orig.note: Sanskrit: fire, and the god of fire. Sita calls on Agni as her witness before stepping into the flames.
